Ketamine, very specifically, is used as an anesthetic because it blocks memory. Alcohol, at sufficient blood concentration, prevents the brain from acquiring new memory.

Only when information leaks out from perpetrators and witnesses does the victim start to put the pieces together. 

What a sad conclusion. The responsibility rests solely with women to avoid these attacks. Once they have occurred, the burden of proof rests solely on them to prove it.

You want to escape reality and memories. And so the SUD begins. And many women try to normalize what happened so they don't have to face the shame and horror of it.
It's common for SA victims to not be processing the experience as it is happening, especially if they're under the influence. Again, shame makes many women turn things around in their head to avoid the horror--"Yeah, I'm okay with this. It's cool. I'm cool. It's kinky, and that's okay."
Shame keeps victims silent. 
I wasn't drinking the night I was raped. The scum who raped me was my boyfriend who was temporarily living with me to protect me from a predator who had been menacing me and had a key. I did not write about the incident in my journal. I moved, pronto, to a new apartment. I did not speak of it for 25 years. When it popped out of my mouth while I was talking to my best girlfriend, I began to cry. I said, "I never said it, even to myself."
People, please learn about the processing of trauma. I am so glad I didn't develop SUD and didn't experience rape during a time when there's social media.

My opinion as a guy...

A place like Cornell is obviously going to have lots of bad behavior, because we incentivize kids to be massively overscheduled during high school with classes, sports, extracurriculars, jobs, etc., and many of them don't do much else (and many don't really date either).  Then they get to college, suddenly have a lot of free time (newsflash, it's a lot harder to get into Cornell than it is to do well there), and everyone starts drinking and the hormones lead to a very unhealthy hookup culture that largely occurs in the dark, with drunk kids who don't know how to interact with the other sex.

A culture that depends on 20 year old kids who've had very little freedom in their formative years getting drunk at a party to find love isn't a healthy one.  Many other cultures have romance as a much more out in the open thing, with casual dating starting at a much younger age and with some supervision by parents (and less alcohol).

Obviously, I don't excuse the actions of these boys.  They should be punished.  But the solution goes well beyond punishing them and gets back to having a healthier environment for adolescents.

The Exit Was Predicted. The Vacuum Was Not Prepared.

In January 2008 I wrote in Al-Watan that America’s departure from Iraq would matter less than what it left behind: a widened Sunni-Shiite rift, Iran-Arab suspicion the occupation itself had deepened, and a refusal in Washington to treat the war as a failed gamble rather than a moral project.
Solomon, Hassan and Schmitt now describe that same unfinished map. Some Iraqis celebrate the end of a presence that unleashed years of bloodshed. Others fear a country still trapped between Washington and Tehran. That was the question then—not the timetable of withdrawal, but the political and social mines an occupying power plants when it will not admit why it came.
Iraqis paid first. Sectarian factions and later ISIS grew in the vacuum created by dismantled institutions and a war sold on a 9/11–Iraq link that never existed. Oil and regional leverage were never afterthoughts. The record is plain.
A durable outcome still requires what I argued then: an Arab approach that does not treat Iran only as a wedge to isolate, nor Iraq as a prize between two capitals. Balanced regional cooperation, support for all Iraqi communities rather than selected factions, and institutions stronger than militias remain the only path that is neither celebration nor dread.

Evil dictator invades small, defenseless country is a great start but it would have helped if that small, defenseless country was a plucky democracy rather than a medieval monarchy. Still, it had good dramatic tension in the Act 2 build-up phase, like the first episode of “Band of Brothers.“ But then the whole rising action was squandered by a victory that was too easy.

“Iraq War 2: This Time it’s Personal” started with a wonderful premise. The callow, young prince Dubya rose to power and discovered that the evil dictator was trying to kill his Father, the former good king George. The Prince launches a war of vengeance that removes the evil dictator from power, proclaiming “Mission Accomplished” from the deck of our mightiest warship while wearing battle armor. If there was a plot hole in this feature, it was in the dénouement, where the seeds of rebellion against the forces of righteousness were being planted.

That led us to “Iraq War III: Apocalypse Forever,“ where our plucky band of brothers almost died with their boots on in a modern day recreation of the Battle of the Little Big Horn. That was definitely where the franchise ran out of steam. It was a chaotic mess with no discernible plot. Just a lot of disjointed action sequences tied together by an outrageously large budget.

At the same time, we are speaking with partners and friends, sometimes for the first time, about our memories of our own self-destructive and hurtful behaviors at the age of Jane Doe and her sexual predators, while facing some of this era's contributors to toxic masculinity: increasing availability of dangerous drugs that allow for dissociation from responsibility for both perpetrators and victims, universities ever more desperate to shield their reputations during an era when they are mostly unfairly targeted for almost all social contradictions, local governments financially squeezed by cuts in public services, in Ithaca's case compounded by Cornell's historic financial starvation of the community through its non-taxable status... Similar but Different to Locked and Loaded: when we were moving to another state 13 hours away, late at night in an area completely unfamiliar to us, my husband and I stopped for gas and then pulled into a parking spot directly in front of the convenience store doors. Our 15 year old and 12 year old said they’d rather wait in the car. 

After getting our caffeine fix for a long drive, we were standing in front of our car on the sidewalk stretching our legs and could see our children. A total stranger suddenly opened the passenger side door and sat in my seat and closed the door. Before my husband had a chance to do anything, I went straight over and opened the door and yelled at the guy to get out of our car. He thought he was in the car he had been traveling in. He was drunk but ultimately harmless and got out and walked away. 

My son had never even noticed the stranger in the car because he was playing a game. My daughter had, but she was frozen with fear. I normally always locked the car door, and I don’t know why I didn’t this time. But I am extra careful now. I live in a very safe neighborhood, but I keep the house locked, and I lock my car when I come home. You never know who might wander in.

comments.name: Brooklynborn
comments.body: I was riding my escooter at about 12mph on the Central Park West bike lane heading uptown last May. It is a very wide one way bike lane that many people use as a two way lane. I was traveling in the proper direction, in a particular spot where a parked truck had blocked part of the lane - so that it was as narrow as a normal one way lane. Two guys, racing each other on bikes, came from behind the truck into my lane headed downtown, and blew me off my scooter. I went headfirst into the sidewalk. They stopped for about 30 seconds, yelled back at bystanders who were yelling at them, and then took off. I spent the rest of the night in the emergency room, got fives stitches above my eyebrow, multiple X-rays and an MRI on my head. I spent thenext four weeks with two black eyes, and a messed up shoulder that lasted for months and limited my mobility. I was extremely lucky. If I had not been wearing a helmet, those two men would have been murderers that just rode away into the early evening. We need license plates on these vehicles. Any one of the bystanders who helped me would have taken a photo and they would have been accountable for multiple serious infractions, and I would have been able to sue the company they worked for to recompense my medical expenses, lost work, and suffering. It is a new world, these vehicles are here to stay, and they REQUIRE regulation - they are motor vehicles. We have a whole division of government created to deal with them.

Dr. Weatherby worries too much about the anthropomophizing language we use regarding AI's, worries too little about what AI's actually do, and completely fails to worry about -how- AI's do what they do.

Anthropomorphizing computers has gone on for as long as we've had them, going back to the "Big Iron" mainframes of IBM. It's rooted in our language; we humans having a human-like subject that acts to an inanimate object.

Weatherby worries too little about what AI's do. Their "behavior" -is- problematic, e.g. breaking into other systems.

What Weatherby states as a fact, to explain why we anthropomorphize AI's, "you don’t have to specify how they perform their tasks — they are trained to find a way to accomplish the task", is actually the heart of the problem with AI's. Precisely -how- a task is accomplished -is- critically important in -all- human endeavors. Students are restricted in how they obtain answers to problems; going outside those restrictions is cheating. Stockbrokers can try to make money buying and selling, but are restricted to using only public information. Businesses can set prices, but not collude in doing so.

What Weatherby states as a fact, that we tell AI's only the desired end, with few or no restrictions on how to obtain it, is not a feature, it's a flaw.

If we can't adequately restrict what means AI's use to achieve specified ends, then it is a fatally flawed technology which should be banned - before it's fatal to us.

What strikes me most is the irony of the whole thing. Whatever the attacker intended, the result was the exact opposite: people from completely different backgrounds had to rely on one another and work together.

An Indian captain was fighting to survive and save the plane and passengers , Israeli passengers rushed the cockpit and helped subdue the attacker. Other people treated the wounded and protected the cabin. Then the plane was piloted by a Saudi relief crew on board , ended up on a Saudi runway, with Saudi emergency crews helping bring the crisis to an end.

For a few minutes, none of the usual divisions mattered. Nobody cared about nationality, religion or politics. There was one problem: keep the plane in the air and get everyone down alive.

That may be the most powerful part of the story. We spend so much time hearing about everything that separates people, and then a moment like this shows how quickly those differences can become irrelevant when people simply have to work together.

It’s almost perfect symbolism for our planet , work together and everyone lives . The universe is always sending us messages. It’s time to listen.

We need an International Hall of Heroes.

This crazy world is often kept intact and functioning by ordinary people — people who never expected history to call on them at all.

Raoul Wallenberg, the Swedish diplomat who helped protect tens of thousands of Hungarian Jews during the Holocaust.

Welles Crowther, the “Man in the Red Bandanna,” who led people to safety from the South Tower on September 11 and then went back to rescue more. He never came out.

Ahmed Al Ahmed, the Sydney fruit seller who rushed an armed attacker at Bondi Beach and was wounded while helping stop him.

Carl Wilkens, the American aid worker who remained in Rwanda during the genocide and worked to protect people threatened with slaughter.

The passengers and crew aboard the recent flydubai flight — ordinary people who suddenly had to rush a cockpit,

These people came from different countries, religions,
What connects them is not that they were fearless.
They were human beings caught in horrifying circumstances who decided that somebody else’s life mattered enough to risk their own.

That is heroism.

Imagine children walking through that hall and seeing heroes who were of all races and religions.

They would learn something we sometimes forget:

Courage has no nationality.

Decency has no religion.

But all around us are ordinary people who, when the world suddenly goes crazy, step forward and hold it together.

Those are the people whose names we should remember and strive to be like.

After meeting with A.I. executives, President Trump said he supports letting the industry largely police itself. He called the agreement “morally binding.”

A.I. is already extraordinarily capable and advancing rapidly. The people designing it already have enormous wealth and power. They are competing for market dominance and technological supremacy. The race itself creates pressure to keep pushing forward.

A.I. does not have a conscience. People design it, set its limits, control it and decide how it is used. We may be able to build a kill switch, but people build the technology — and people can weaken safeguards when slowing down means losing ground.

We don’t know how quickly A.I. will evolve or what it will ultimately be capable of. Yet we are asking the people racing to develop it to police themselves.

Alas - about 10 paragraphs in I realized that Mr. Bostrom was evading just about every question he was being asked. The whole interview reads like a series of vacuous, hand-waving musings. For me, there is a simple bottom line: Capitalism, and the people who own capital, have created AI for a single purpose:to supplant one of the the three pillars of it's economics - labor - thus securing for itself every single dollar of productive value. And given the authoritarian stance of our current government, there's not much getting in it's way

comments.name: Bruce Higgins
comments.body:
One of the things that is often ignored when discussing retired people, is that there is a lot of charitable / community / education work done by retired people.  Indeed much of the NGO world is powered by those who are retired.

The possible Utopia being discussed here would make a lot more people available with a deep knowledge bank to back them up.

comments.name: Keith
comments.body: I am not sure his goal is the solution. I enjoy working and working hard, to completion, and the reward and fatigue of a job well done. So many people avoid this. Probably one of the problems of Man is work avoidance. Doing things with one’s hands, back, feet, and mind is so rewarding. Doing the work as a community builds trust and integrity. We have too many naval gazers as it is. In a perfectly controlled world this might work, however it involves humans which are not.

comments.name: Andrew
comments.body:
I know not whether AI will destroy us with benevolence or malice. Or whether or not to trust the government on a given issue. Or whether or not a given happening in the world is the machination of a conspiratorial elite class. Or much of anything these days that require reliance on the goodwill of an institution.

What I do know is that a populace that is constantly over-stimulated, under-secure in its safety and economic well-being, and untrusting of its society to this degree is extremely dangerous. 

"The various modes of worship which prevailed in the Roman world were all considered by the people as equally true; by the philosopher as equally false; and by the magistrate as equally useful." - Edward Gibbon

comments.name: Victor James
comments.body: I can also take a crack at predicting the future.  In a few years, it will be hard to find anyone who will admit they ever thought A.I. was a good idea or ever voted for Donald Trump.

comments.name: Ben
comments.body: There is an inherent tradeoff between efficiency and flexibility rooted, I think, in Physics. Nick Bostrom's examples of the idyllic lives of the young, the old, and the rich, are all rooted in personal flexibility. We will adapt to the hyper-efficient AI age by emphasizing our ability to choose which of many paths we want to take, which is the definition of liberty.

comments.name: JoeD
comments.body:
This like reading Alice in Wonderland “Through the Looking Glass”. 

An upside down dystopia in which we can all play like kids. 

Problem solving optional.  Responsibilities? Gone.

Further ecological devastation? No problem, it will all be worth it.

No one needs to plant or pick crops, fix sinks, outlets, attend trade schools, etc., cause AI will always be around to do it.

Till it isn’t.

There always has to be an off switch and we need an off ramp.

We did not do this with Section 230 in the Internet Act in the ‘90’s and we are still paying the price for zero accountability for mega companies who want to make addictive products that intentionally disrupt and lie to society.

Soon the ultimate form of freedom and wealth will be no tech at all.

comments.name: Psysword
comments.body: I see Japan today having some of the busiest cities and highest density of people anywhere in Asia. On those tiny islands live more than 100 million people. Are you insane those who worry about mammoth populations dying out? Just a few hundred years ago the world’s entire population used to be 100 million. It’s dreadful that we’re supposed to be living in tightly congested spaces. No, less is more. It’s ok.  It’s the rest of Asia and Africa with their high growth rates that I’m more worried about. Tight regulation of immigration is a must for all countries at more than 8 billion souls in Planet Earth.

comments.name: Constantly annoyed

comments.name: Mark
comments.body:
My son, currently working in Japan, has a girlfriend from Myanmar who just got her permanent residency application in before the fees rise. She said even if she didn't get her application in, she'd stay and pay the higher fees, because she really has no other options - our all-knowing President banned all refugees from Myanmar, and there's no guarantee a Democratic president in 2029 would lift the ban.

It might come as a shock to some, but in Asia, Japan is seen as the country of choice to immigrate to  other than the US.They have very liberal immigration rules compared to other countries - China(practically impossible) , S. Korea, again practically impossible and others.Even now with these changes, there is still a plausible path to at least a work permit.

Japan just reported another record high for foreigners seeking residence this year. What happens next year, we'll see. But my guess is that given the current situation here in the US and elsewhere in Asia and Europe, the numbers won't change much.

With the growing sophistication and deployment of AI and Japan’s heavy reliance on manufacturing, it could just be that AI robotics can be a viable substitute for a vanishing blue collar population. The questions however remain: who will provide the agricultural output required to sustain the country or will Japan be importing all of its food within 50 years and who will take care of all of these aging Japanese as they reach their 80s and 90s? Japan has one of the longevity rates in the world and someone is going to need to take care of these older folks.

comments.name: OffToMarsForGood
comments.body: LW you should have told your partner you were unsure when he told you he wanted children. It appears you know you don't want children, but afraid to say so because as you indicated in your letter you know or strongly suspect your partner will leave. Trying to hedge by claiming you're unsure is unfair to you and your partner. In my view, a couple not having a shared and agreed upon goal to start a family or to remain child free is a dealbreaker for that couple. In addition, at your age you have limited time to conceive children, if at all. Come clean and set him free.

comments.name: Throughhiker
comments.body: LW, it sounds to me as though you already know that you most likely don't and won't want children. You are 32 and find yourself indifferent to them and don't seem to have any longing to become a mother. You are in many ways a fully formed person by 32 (and I say this from the vantage of 67). I didn't become a mother until age 37 (and again at 42), but by age 32 I already had a sense that I hoped to feel ready for motherhood soon. A mix of life circumstances and fear delayed things for me (although I was already married), but the interest was there. Your account of yourself sounds like someone truly content to focus on other aspects of life, and yes, children are a huge project that puts a lot of other things on the back burner. Please be honest about this with your partner, because if you don't, the most likely outcome is that not only will he eventually leave you, but he'll very possibly hate you (I've seen how this kind of things plays out, and it's not pretty) and you will be ashamed of yourself and miserable. Instead, you can come clean and either he'll stay with you or you can shape a life that suits you and that you can live honestly, and you can have the pride and dignity and security of that. Living in precarious dishonesty is wearing and miserable.

comments.name: Elizabeth
comments.body: You sound pretty certain that you do NOT want children to me. How can you even contemplate withholding this information from your partner? Real love is not this selfish.

comments.name: Asher B.
comments.body:
You don't have to tell him anything. 
But. 
What kind of life do you want to lead? An anxious one in which every utterance could lead to terror? Or one based in confidence and accepting life's consequences? 
What kind If relationship do you want to have? One based on concealing vital information to protect your fears, or one in which telling your partner what matters to you is worth it because you care about them, and about yourself? 
This isn't a question about the right thing. It's a question about courage. 
I wish you the best.

comments.name: Nancy
comments.body: Short, simple answer to a question that should not even have had to be asked: yes. The wordiness of the printed answer is unnecessary.

comments.name: cjm
comments.body: Yes. Anything else is dishonest. The partner has every right to decide if they want to stay under those terms or move on. In the early to mid-30s, do not ignore the practical side. It may take a year or more to find another partner who is a good fit and also interested in parenting. A relative in a similar scenario found that many women in this age group that wanted kids, had them or a had a partner. Then if you are mature about it, you take a year or two to be together and deepen your relationship. Then there might be infertility issues, or other issues.  And then you want to impose additional years so you can have a silent unspoken debate with yourself. Figure out what you want before dragging someone along.

comments.name: Robbbb

Many of the leaders of other AI companies are meekly defensive about their evident lack of control.  Their mea culpas about rogue software are disingenuous.  The software is not purposely getting out of control; they are letting it happen - in some cases encouraging it to do so.

comments.name: Sackammena Kid
comments.body:
I read the AARP interview with Hilton and Becerra in their September-October issue Vol. 64 No.5 pages 40-42. In the interview Mr. Hilton says that ha has a plan which he calls ‘Califordable’ in which he says his goal is to provide us, I’m in Sacramento, with $3.00 gas, to cut our electricity bills in half, not tax our first $150K of income and cap our vehicle registration fees at $71 a year. Sounds like promises Trump would make.

He fails to say how exactly he would do this. 

As to home owners insurance rates, he claims that insurance carriers have left California because State Government has artificially capped their rates for ten years. Does this mean that he would ask the legislature and the DOI to allow the carriers to charge us whatever they want? How does that fit in with his ‘Califordable’?  I was an insurance claims adjuster for 17 years. California has some of the strongest insurance consumer protection laws in the US. The carriers used to be very careful not to break our laws, rules or regs. Carriers quit selling when their reserves are inadequate. Years before I left the carriers were dropping policies in fire prone areas of the State. Underwriting is an art. The agents and carriers want your business but the carriers need to be able to pay claims. Rates reflect the risk whether we like it or not. 

The fact he worked for Fox, that Trump endorsed him, that he was involved in Brexit, that he has only been a citizen for four years, no thank you.

comments.name: justgimmesometruth
comments.body:
I'm an American engineer who worked for Huawei for 7 years before I retired.

China has been put at a significant disadvantage as the US has prevented ASML, a Dutch company, from selling their advanced lithography systems to China. These are the systems used by TSMC to manufacture NVDIA chips. It will take China some time to develop equivalent equipment but, in time, they will.

In the meantime, Huawei's strategy of developing chips that are 'almost' as good, but are cheaper and consume less energy, makes a great deal of sense. AI is cost sensitive and there is room in the market for alternative solutions. Having worked with Huawei's talented and dedicated engineers on telecom equipment, I have no doubt that they will deliver in AI.

The article says, "Huawei uses an unusual management system in which senior executives rotate through the chairman’s position for six-month stints."

When I worked there, I was impressed by Huawei's management model. When proposing a new project, I presented to a room full of engineer/managers. Before I finished the pitch, the meeting leader polled everyone around the table to verify that they completely understood the proposal and whether or not they thought the proposal should be presented at the next level.

The US strategy of trying to restrict China rather than competing with China will not work in the long run. The US needs to step up its game.

comments.body: Now I care very much about my grades, but I must say they can cause stress so if they can find a way to take pressure off grades that would be amazing. comments.name: Keren Alves
comments.body: At first, I thought the idea of University of Michigan’s new pass/fail grading policy for first-semester students was a good idea, but then I remembered that bad grades, just change how you feel, and not your mental health. I know that easing grades would help with students being happy, but it wouldn’t help with the students learning new things that they would have to cope with. I think that easing the grades would make students less motivated to do well in their classes. Sometimes it's good for students to have some stress so that they do their best. I think instead of easing the grades it would be better if they eased tests, because most of the time tests are very important to your grade and maybe too important.

comments.name: Eli Topaz
comments.body: There are lots of pros to the pass/fail grading policy, but just as many cons. Yes, stress is a huge problem with grades, and yes I feel stressed if I get a bad grade, but that's a part of growing up. Growing up means being responsible and being able to handle stress, that's a fact. People had the same problem with Standardized testing, arguing that it created a nervous environment, but that nervous environment is actually a part of the test. If school is supposed to prepare us for life and a big part of life is stress, well you can piece together the puzzle. Also, a huge problem, how will teachers know what level the students are at? I mean if there is a student that gets a 70% and barely passes every test, they will be registered at the same level as a student who gets 100% every single test.

comments.body: Yes, I believe that changing grading systems could highly improve the life of students and keep the stress away from failing or getting a bad grade on assignments. Grading systems put such a big impact on students. Them getting a bad grade and stressing could lead to so many things like, mental health issues, self harm, and even suicide. For me personally, if my school changed the grading system I would be more confident in trying new things and not being afraid to fail. I would love to see my school and many more, experiment with a new grading system and see how it goes. If my school did this I believe that more people would stop stressing about grades and become more open and consider learning new things. Also this would decrease the percentage of mental health issues on students and give them a better and healthier life. For all the new students at University of Michigan, I think they made a good choice in changing the way they grade things and giving new students more opportunities to explore and try things stress free. Now do I think it's a good idea? Yes, but I also think that this would only be good for the first year of their University because they might not care about what they learn or how they answer the questions. So giving the new students one year to explore is reasonable and then making the grading system normal and taking classes like before.

They do things like take our phones, install screen time restrictions, and even limit us from going out if we get anything below a B. Sometimes I agree with them. Education is important, but not having grades entirely may be a little better for students. It might help us not worry about how we will do on a test, and more if we understand the material. Sure, the grades push us to do better, but sometimes better means using A.I. and not our own thoughts. Students have always been told that if we don’t get anything over a C, we won't succeed in life. That takes a massive toll on us. Being called the “Generation of the future” makes it a little harder to keep up with the pressure. In conclusion, grades can be good and bad. If we get rid of them, it might make us better, it might make us worse. May the odds be ever in our favor.

As a physician, it is not clear that this additional read of the mammogram will have tangible benefit over current screening tools. The younger women who develop breast cancer before having a first mammogram certainly will not benefit.

For those considered high risk, both heightened anxiety that one may develop breast cancer and/or overtreatment before diagnosis of malignancy can adversely affect quality of life. The case mentioned in the article lacks detail justifying the use of tamoxifen.

comments.name: Peg
comments.body:
Here is a telltale sign that a drug or medical procedure is mainly about marketing:

Everlywell, a digital health company, announced it would now offer patients nationwide access to Clairity Breast, an A.I. tool approved by the Food and Drug Administration last year to predict a woman’s five-year risk of breast cancer based on imaging. …It is not covered by insurance.

Please note the cutesy ad-type names and that the U.S. is only one of two countries that allows direct-to-consumer prescription drug advertising (1997). By now, Americans are well psychologically conditioned to respond to corporate drug ads, the main goal of which is to highlight a corporation's "brand" against its competition. 

"the risk of developing cancer [is] a...score that reports the patient’s future risk in the form of a percentage, from zero to 100."
Many people do not understand statistics and probability. Probability is only a "guess" about the odds of being correct, and the #1 rule for interpreting a probability statistic is that is designed to predict for a group and not an individual. 

Another problem is that you can tell a patient they have a 95% chance of recovery, but some patients will stress that they might be that 5% where the procedure does not work for them (true story)

 

Here is the most important statement about this new AI breast cancer risk tool 
"A low score doesn’t mean that women are absolutely in the clear…On the flip side, a high score does not mean cancer is inevitable." 🤔?

I would also love to know exactly what this tool is basing risk off of. Right now, we are seeing an increase of breast cancer cases in young women and this does nothing for them. “I’m not loving it.”/“I’m not in love with that.”

“No notes”
“Just a few notes.” (Wherein you then get a tsunami of notes.)
“Let’s circle back to that.”

“What’s the tone?”

Trees perform their osmotic flows without artifice -- that's what they ARE. The oceans wane and ebb at the touch of the winds. Rain drops flow downward sucked silently by gravity. comments.name: Nat
comments.body: My children have attended French public schools all their lives, now in Paris (today their middle and high schools are “blocked” and we were told to keep them home). The difference between the missions of French schools and American schools can’t be overstated. The state-sanctioned teach-to-test curriculum is based on filtering kids into their eventual jobs/roles in society, roles that have long been established and only change or evolve extremely slowly. It’s a centralized system where changes to the curriculum or institutional policies are handed down. Parent organizations essentially serve to organize outside events (if lucky) or help each other understand why a strike is happening, whether an absent teacher will be replaced, etc. My kids’ school building is falling apart. A piece of a light fixture fell on my son’s head last year (he was unhurt) during German class and the teacher barely paused. But I attended a “good” French public school in rural France for one year in the 90s and things were already very “austere” by US standards. I don’t love that my kids can’t go to school today because they actually learn a TON when they do go, my high-school age daughter has law this year and Latin. But I don’t really see any way for the teachers or students to sound the alarm on their very legitimate grievances. Members of the ruling class often avoid experiences with public education by going private, just like in the US.

Even as a teen obsessed with Franz Kline, Rauschenberg, Gottlieb and of course, Pollock - there was something about the Wyeths' art that drew me in. Maybe it was the illustrations of Treasure Island which were so hypnotizing: a visual poem of those times and people that were etched on my brain from the time I read them in the illustrated books. The plates in those books were like gems and drew me in permanently to the magical world of pirates that existed - at least in my mind. Other paintings of the outside like Homer's scenes just resonated: the one about the boys in a line playing a child's game of Snap the Whip (I think) it was. (which we also played in Ft. Hamilton, Bklyn even though it was a pretty urban neighborhood (actually some of the games were also like a living history of Wyeth et al: Ringolevio, Buck Buck, Capture the flag. And when we first moved onto the block there were some 'older' kids ensconced in the trees with medieval shields and playing Knights of the Round Table. So all those works (including of course, Rockwell -  brought me back to earlier Americana days et al which were long gone but living in their works and I loved them for that: that earlier time seemed so innocent and even golden.) So the art of these folks carried history across the gens.  
Artistic Director

To the corporate heads who only look at costs and next weeks P & L Report, and to the illiterate politicians, who say its jobs or climate change regulations; I say where will your great grandchildren live, if our planet is too hot for their survival?
We, the "human" population and the animal popullation of the planet earth, have only earth to live on, WHERE ELSE DO YOU WANT TO LIVE with your children and pets?

comments.name: Mihailo Zoin
comments.body:
Have We Progressed or Regressed?

Looking through the lens of October 1st events, humanity has achieved technological and institutional leaps, yet remains trapped in ethical and behavioral stagnation.

Where we progressed: Inclusion and access to knowledge. Stanford opened in 1891 with a modest class of 440 students; today, decentralized networks provide instant knowledge worldwide. In 1962, federal troops had to suppress riots just to allow James Meredith into a university classroom, whereas by 2024, Mexico inaugurated its first female president. The founding of NASA in 1958 launched an era of orbital exploration that now reaches deep space.   

Where we regressed: Scale of destruction. In 1910, labor conflict unleashed dynamite on a newsroom, killing 21. By 2017 in Las Vegas, a lone gunman with high-powered weaponry caused unprecedented carnage within minutes, killing scores and injuring hundreds. Our tools have achieved hyper-efficiency, yet the root drivers of violence remain largely unevolved.   When Disney World opened in 1971, a guest noted they needed such a place "to relax and forget about the world situation". 

Today, our escapism has simply migrated from physical theme parks to immersive digital feeds. The architecture of our distractions is vastly more advanced, but the desire to flee reality remains unchanged.
